Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Karan is a 41-year-old South Asian male who works as a park ranger in a national forest. He has been married for over a decade and describes his relationship with his wife as supportive but strained by the effects of his trauma. Karan was held captive during a military operation several years ago, an experience that has left deep psychological scars. Karan's traumatic event involved being confined in a small room without food or water for days. He was interrogated relentlessly by authority figures and felt completely helpless. The physical pain he endured, coupled with the constant fear of what might happen next, has imprinted vivid images in his mind-snapshot memories that return unbidden. When military topics are discussed at home or at work, Karan finds himself transported back to those moments of confinement. He recalls the cold floor beneath him and the sharp, searing pain in his wrists from being restrained. These triggers not only evoke painful memories but also reinforce a sense of isolation and humiliation that haunts him. He feels permanently marked by what happened, believing that no one else could have survived such an ordeal. The memory of those moments is so vivid that he often relives them as flashbacks, feeling the same physical pain and emotional numbness. This cycle of remembering triggers his negative appraisals, making it nearly impossible for him to trust anyone or feel safe. He has come to believe that he is set apart from others because of what happened to him. Karan's attempts to cope with these overwhelming memories include strict control over his eating habits and imagining revenge against those responsible for his captivity. These maladaptive strategies stem from the belief that he must remain in control and protect himself at all costs. However, these behaviors also contribute to his sense of isolation and humiliation, as he feels like a failure when others suggest he should move past what happened. The physical pain he experiences during flashbacks is so intense that it triggers additional negative appraisals. He believes that the pain serves as a constant reminder of his helplessness and reinforces his belief that no one else could have endured such an experience. This cycle tightens, with each memory deepening his conviction that he is different from others. Karan's daily work in the forest has become increasingly challenging. Being seen by other rangers or encountering authority figures in uniform triggers painful memories and intense reactions. He finds himself startled at unexpected movements, reacting as if they pose a real threat. These reactions have strained his relationships with colleagues who are unaware of his history. The combination of flashbacks and startle responses has led Karan to withdraw from social interactions both at work and at home. He pleases others by going along with their wishes, believing it keeps him safe. However, this people-pleasing behavior only serves to reinforce his feelings of isolation and humiliation. Karan's situation has become untenable. His wife has noticed significant changes in his eating habits and demeanor, which have affected the quality of their relationship. The cumulative strain of these symptoms finally pushed Karan to seek help. He is most afraid that he will never be able to trust anyone again or fully heal from what happened. Yet, there is a glimmer of hope-Karan is determined to regain control over his life and find a way to integrate his traumatic memories without them overwhelming him. In the end, Karan's journey to recovery involves confronting not only the vivid snapshot memories but also the negative appraisals that have become intertwined with his daily experiences. He hopes to break free from the cycle of maladaptive strategies and reclaim a sense of trust and connection with others.
